title: The Slow Postcards
premise: Noor Coldharbour, a piano tuner who reads a building's past through its radiators and pipes, has spent thirty years keeping an inventory of everything unsaid—about her brother's disappearance, about the fire in the old neighborhood, about what she traded for silence. When Ilma Vask, the last fluent speaker of a dying language, asks Noor to become her final student, the lessons begin unearthing words Noor buried: her brother's name, the night he vanished, and the neighbor everyone blamed. As the city reroutes the last bus to the old quarter, Noor must return to the ruined house where the story went wrong, testify to what she actually saw, and choose loyalty to the living over loyalty to the lie. The novel ends with Noor speaking the truth aloud in Ilma's dying language at a public inquiry, her brother's name restored to the record, and the bus route preserved—not as a victory, but as the first honest sentence in a new inventory.
about_author: Ulyana Vane is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing other people's truths before writing her own. She lives above a defunct music shop and claims she can still hear the building dreaming through its pipes.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: POV Noor. In her meticulous notebooks, Noor catalogs the silences of her clients' homes and her own flat, establishing her ritual of listening to radiators. A commission at a condemned building unsettles her; she recognizes the address and closes the notebook early. Emotional beat: controlled dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: Ilma Vask Asks
chapters.summary: POV Noor. At the community hall, the last speaker of Vaskari, an elderly woman, publicly asks Noor—of all people—to be her final student. Noor refuses on the spot, then cannot sleep. The request feels less like flattery than a summons. Emotional beat: the terror of being seen.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Tuning a piano in the old neighborhood's surviving row houses, Noor hears through the pipes the echo of the night her brother Tomas vanished—boots, shouting, a door. She flees mid-job. Emotional beat: memory breaking through craft like water through plaster.

chapters.title: The First Lesson
chapters.summary: POV Noor, with Ilma. Noor returns to Ilma's kitchen, telling herself she'll decline properly. Instead Ilma begins with a single word meaning both 'house' and 'what holds you.' Noor repeats it and hears her own voice shake. Emotional beat: reluctant surrender to the first honest word.

chapters.title: The Man Everyone Blamed
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Noor encounters Denny Rook, the neighbor convicted decades ago for the fire that preceded Tomas's disappearance, now paroled and working the demolition crew. His calm terrifies her more than anger would. Emotional beat: guilt wearing a familiar face.

chapters.title: Words That Have No Alibi
chapters.summary: POV Noor, with Ilma. Ilma teaches Vaskari words for truths the legal language lacks—'to carry another's sentence.' Noor realizes Ilma knows more about the old case than she's admitted. Emotional beat: the suspicion that her teacher is also an interrogator.

chapters.title: The Last Bus Notice
chapters.summary: POV Noor. The transit authority posts notice: the 47 route to the old quarter will be permanently rerouted in six weeks. The neighborhood's last thread to the city will be cut. Noor clips the notice into her inventory. Emotional beat: a deadline made physical.

chapters.title: Denny's Version
chapters.summary: POV Denny. Rook, wary and plain-spoken, tells Noor he never touched the fire or the boy, and that someone's silence convicted him. He doesn't ask her to confess—only to remember correctly. Emotional beat: the unbearable courtesy of the wronged.

chapters.title: The Night, Reassembled
chapters.summary: POV Noor. In fragmented flashback, the fire, the crowd, fourteen-year-old Noor watching from the stairwell, and Tomas running toward the burning house—not away from it. What she told the police and what she saw split into two records. Emotional beat: the fracture that made her a keeper of silences.

chapters.title: Ilma's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Noor, with Ilma. Ilma admits she was the one who urged the community to name a culprit quickly, to protect someone—she never says whom. She wants Noor as a student because Noor is the only living witness. Emotional beat: teacher and student bound by shared complicity.

chapters.title: The House on Vask Street
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Noor enters the condemned house she's avoided for thirty years. The radiators still hold sound: her brother's voice, a second voice she has spent her life not identifying. She recognizes it now—her father's. Emotional beat: the floor giving way beneath the family myth.

chapters.title: What Fathers Burn
chapters.summary: POV Noor, flashback-heavy. Reconstruction of the truth: her father started the fire for insurance, Tomas discovered it, and the father let the neighborhood's rage fall on Denny Rook while Noor, a child, was coached into silence. Emotional beat: grief with nowhere to be placed.

chapters.title: The Inventory Burns
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Noor rereads thirty years of notebooks and finds every entry bent around the same omission. She burns the old volumes in her sink—not erasure, she tells herself, but clearing the page. Emotional beat: destructive relief.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV Noor, with her dying mother. Noor visits her mother, who still defends the father's memory. Noor almost tells her, then doesn't, and understands the cost of both choices. Emotional beat: love and truth as competing debts.

chapters.title: The Inquiry Notice
chapters.summary: POV Noor. A reinvestigation of the Rook conviction opens, prompted by Ilma's formal statement. A lawyer contacts Noor as a material witness. Her refusal window is closing. Emotional beat: the past acquiring legal teeth.

chapters.title: Denny at the Door
chapters.summary: POV Denny. Rook comes to Noor's flat, not to pressure her but to give her something Tomas left in his keeping that night: a notebook of the boy's own, documenting the fire's cause. Emotional beat: the dead brother testifying at last.

chapters.title: Tomas's Handwriting
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Reading Tomas's notebook, Noor hears his voice for the first time in thirty years—angry, funny, afraid. She practices saying the truth in Vaskari with Ilma, word by word, as if learning to walk. Emotional beat: language as resurrection.

chapters.title: The Last Ordinary Day
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Before everything changes, Noor tunes one final piano, walks the route of the 47 bus, and says goodbye to her invisibility like an old coat. Emotional beat: tender, deliberate farewell.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: POV Noor. At the inquiry, Noor testifies: the fire's cause, her father's role, Tomas's discovery, the coached silence. Her voice holds. Denny Rook weeps without sound. Emotional beat: climax—the body shaking as truth leaves it.

chapters.title: Aftermath, in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: POV Noor, with Ilma. The conviction is vacated; the father, long dead, is named in the record. Ilma, failing fast, asks Noor to recite what she's learned. Noor speaks Tomas's story in Vaskari, and Ilma calls her fluent. Emotional beat: grief and transmission in one breath.

chapters.title: The Route Preserved
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Community testimony—Noor's among it—wins the 47 bus a reprieve as a heritage route. Denny rides it to the old quarter for the first time as a free man. Emotional beat: quiet, unglamorous justice.

chapters.title: A New Inventory
chapters.summary: POV Noor. Noor begins a fresh notebook, first line: things said. She tunes the condemned house's piano one last time before demolition, plays a note for Tomas, and lets the radiators answer. The last line of the book is the Vaskari word for house. Emotional beat: resolved, open-hearted, listening forward.
